steps.title: Tell Us What's Happening
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to say first: what is slow, blocked or backing up and where; whether it is one sink or toilet or several at once (the trade facts: one fixture points at its own trap and waste, several outlets or the outside chamber point at the shared run); whether the outside chamber is full or overflowing, seen from above without lifting anything; whether next door has the same; how long it has been going on; a photo of the chamber or the wet ground if one can be taken safely. cards.title: A drain that blocks again in the same place
cards.brief: Problem led, the pack's planned register: a blockage back within weeks or months at the same spot, a chamber that fills again after use, several drains slow at once (Table B drain unblocking, tree root removal and CCTV drain surveys signs rows). The one cause this card makes: a fault at one point in the pipe that clearing leaves behind: a joint roots have grown through, a cracked or displaced joint, a dip or a flattened section that holds solids (Table B; Table E collapse against ordinary blockage: a repeat at the same place and the camera's footage are what support a structural diagnosis, never the symptom on its own). Say what usually follows, in plain words: the run cleared, then a camera through it so the fault is seen before anything is recommended (Table A drain unblocking: inspected where a defect is suspected); a repair, a patch repair or a liner only off what the footage shows, and sometimes nothing (the pack's craft rule). By category: Drainage Service leads; Plumbing reads it as the drain a plumber's clearing of the trap cannot reach (Table E: one fixture against several outlets or an outside chamber); Sewage Disposal Service as a tank that backs up again after every empty, which points at the outlet or the drainage field (Table B septic tank repairs); Septic Tank Service as a system that keeps failing, where the question is repair or a new tank or plant (the desire led page owns the new system). Never a reline or a dig written as the default answer to a blockage; never a dig at whoever cleared it last; never 'collapsed' from a symptom.
cards.mechanism: a fault at one point in the pipe that clearing leaves behind

cards.title: A smell you can't find the source of
cards.brief: Problem led: a smell from a plughole, a whiff after a flush, a sewage smell beside an outside chamber or a gully, a smell in one room that comes and goes (Table B drain odour investigations and septic tank emptying signs rows). The one cause this card makes: drain air getting out where a seal has failed: a trap that has lost its water seal, so the air in the drain comes straight up the waste, or a leaking or blocked section outside letting it out of the ground (Table B skipped row). Say what finding it involves, from Table A drain odour investigations: where and when the smell comes, the traps, the vents and the accessible chambers checked, the likely route traced, the suspected section put under the camera or tested, then the cause reported before anything is repaired; treating the smell without finding the source leaves the fault (the done badly row). By category: Drainage Service leads; Plumbing reads it as the trap under the fixture and the vent, the plumber's side before the drain; Sewage Disposal Service and Septic Tank Service as a sewage smell at the tank, by the outlet or over the drainage field, a sign of a tank due an empty or a field that is failing (Table B septic tank emptying and repairs signs rows). Never a product poured down the drain as the answer; never rats unless the footage showed them (Table E).
cards.mechanism: drain air getting out where a seal has failed

cards.title: Wet ground, sinking paving or grass greener along one line
cards.brief: Problem led: a patch of ground that stays damp above where a drain runs, paving over the run that has settled, a strip of lawn lush in a dry spell, a smell that goes with it (Table B leak detection, drain repairs and home buyer drain surveys signs rows; the pack's craft rule on green grass marking a leaking drain). The one cause this card makes: water escaping from a pipe underground and taking the soil with it, so the ground above softens or sinks (Table B skipped rows; Table E leaking drains and subsidence: the facts say a leak can wash away or soften soil, never that the house has subsided). Say what finding it involves from Table A leak detection: supply, waste or drain established first, the run traced, the camera or a test on the suspected section, the fault located and recorded, then the repair specified; the repair from Table A drain repairs (the defect located, responsibility settled, a local repair or a patch, the result tested). By category: Plumbing (leak detection) leads; Drainage Service reads it as the repair or the excavation that follows; Sewage Disposal Service and Septic Tank Service as wet ground at a tank's outlet or pooling over the drainage field (Table B septic tank repairs). Whether the home insurer pays for finding or fixing it only as the customer's own policy says (Table E: policies vary, never a promise). Never subsidence as a diagnosis; never a dig before the source is found (Table B leak detection done badly).
cards.mechanism: water escaping from a pipe underground and taking the soil with it

cards.title: Rainwater that has nowhere to go
cards.brief: Problem led, the surface water side: a puddle that stands by a downpipe after every shower, a gully whose grate is packed with leaves and holds water, a corner of the garden that stays waterlogged, water running towards the house (Table B gully cleaning and soakaways signs rows). The one cause this card makes: an outlet silted up, or ground that cannot take the water: silt and leaves in the gully stopping its outlet so the water backs onto the surface, or a soakaway in ground that cannot absorb what the roof sends it, or with the water table reaching it in winter (Table B skipped and done badly rows). Say what putting it right involves from Table A: the gully cleared to its outlet and flushed; for a soakaway, the ground and the groundwater tested before anything is sized, and the test not done in a downpour, a hard frost or a drought because the result would not be true of the ground (Table A soakaways timing); a new soakaway kept away from the house and the road only as the rule rows give it, with 'usually' and never the distance. On Sewage Disposal Service and Septic Tank Service the card reads as rainwater that finds its way into a septic tank or a treatment plant, which the rule rows keep separate from it, said as what usually applies and why (a tank is sized for the house's waste water, not the roof's). Plumbing reads it as the downpipe and the gully the plumber is asked about first. Never a promise the ground will drain; never a claim that the town floods or that drains in the area fail (the pack's section 3).
cards.mechanism: an outlet silted up, or ground that cannot take the water

problem_card.title: Gullies and soakaways in the wet months
problem_card.brief: Say first what is normal: a soakaway that takes longer to empty in a wet winter as the ground around it fills, leaves on every grate in autumn, a drainage field slower when the ground is sodden. Then what is not: a gully that stands full after the rain has stopped, water across the drive or into the house, a downpipe backing up at its foot (Table B gully cleaning and soakaways signs rows). The one cause this card makes: ground full of water and gullies full of leaves, so the rain has nowhere to go (Table B done badly: a high water table stops a soakaway taking water; the skipped row: silt and leaves stopping the outlet). Say what a visit does, from Table A: the gully cleared to its outlet and flushed; a soakaway looked at with its ground and its groundwater, and any test left until the ground is neither flooded nor frozen (Table A soakaways timing). By category: Drainage Service leads; Sewage Disposal Service and Septic Tank Service read it as a drainage field standing wet and rainwater getting into the tank; Plumbing as the downpipe and the gully. cards.title: Sewage coming up outside or indoors
cards.brief: Write the reader's situation, why it can't wait and what they do first, in that order: waste water lifting the lid of the outside chamber, sewage across the path or the lawn, a downstairs shower tray or gully filling when a toilet is flushed upstairs, several outlets backing up at once (Table B emergency drainage and drain unblocking signs rows). The one cause this card makes: the main run blocked, so everything sent down comes back at the lowest opening (Table B skipped row: sewage escapes when the level upstream overtops an opening). What they do first, from the trade facts rows only: keep everyone out of the water and cover any cuts (Table E Weil's disease), pour nothing down the drain (Table E chemical cleaner risk), nobody leans into or climbs down the chamber (Table E confined space entry), and where next door has it too or the chamber is in the road, the water company first (Table E who to call first). Why it can't wait: the longer it runs the further the contamination spreads (Table B skipped row). What usually happens when they call: the hazards looked at, private or public established, the area isolated, the blockage contained or cleared, the flow confirmed and any fault behind it recorded for a repair (Table A emergency drainage). By category: Drainage Service leads; Plumbing reads it as the drain beyond the trap a plumber hands on; Sewage Disposal Service as a pump alarm sounding or a tank backing up into the house (Table B sewage pumps signs row). Never an arrival time, round the clock cover or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time], [CV: out_of_hours_available] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it; never a promise it won't come back.
cards.mechanism: the main run blocked, so everything sent down comes back at the lowest opening

cards.title: The only toilet in the house blocked
cards.brief: The reader's situation: the bowl fills instead of clearing, the flush comes back up, and it is the only toilet they have; or a sink or shower tray standing full of grey water that will not go (Table B blocked toilets and blocked sinks and showers signs rows). The one cause this card makes: an obstruction between the pan or the trap and the drain, with the water above it going nowhere. What they do first, from the trade facts: check whether another toilet, a sink or the outside gully is backing up too, because one fixture points at its own waste and several point at the drain outside (Table E plumbing problem against drain problem), and nothing poured down it (Table E chemical cleaner risk). Why it can't wait: the retained sewage overflows at the next use (Table B skipped row). What usually happens: the other fixtures checked, the pan or the trap and the access downstream inspected, the obstruction removed rather than pushed further in, the discharge tested, and a repeat investigated for a fault in the drain (Table A blocked toilets and blocked sinks and showers; the done badly rows: an obstruction pushed on, a trap put back so it loses its seal). By category: Drainage Service leads; Plumbing reads it as the trap and the waste first, the drain second; Sewage Disposal Service as the first sign a tank or a pump chamber is full. Never a chemical the client values do not give; never 'same day' unless [CV: same_day_available] is yes.
cards.mechanism: an obstruction between the pan or the trap and the drain

cards.title: Water rising in a cellar or across a floor
cards.brief: The reader's situation: standing water indoors that is not going down, a cellar filling, water climbing an inside wall, a flooded drive with a gully under it somewhere (Table B flood water pumping signs row). The one cause this card makes: water coming in faster than any drain can take it away, from a river, the road or a blocked surface water drain. What they do first, from the trade facts: keep clear of water that may carry sewage (Table E), and know that pumping a building out starts when the water outside is lower than the water inside, because emptying it sooner can harm the structure (Table E pumping floodwater), so nobody bails or pumps it themselves before that. Why it can't wait: the longer the water stands against walls and floors the more it damages, and contaminated water is a hazard while it sits (Table B skipped row). What usually happens when they call: the level, the contamination and where the water can be sent assessed, the area protected, a pump set when the outside level permits, the levels watched, the damage recorded (Table A flood water pumping); the water is never pumped to a place that floods or pollutes somewhere else (Table B done badly). By category: Drainage Service leads; Plumbing reads it as a burst or a leak indoors that is the plumber's before the drain; Sewage Disposal Service as a pump chamber overtopping. Never a promise about the flood, the river or the council's drains; a flood history only from the dossier.
cards.mechanism: water coming in faster than any drain can take it away

cards.title: Who to call first, and what not to do while you wait
cards.brief: The reader's situation: sewage or water somewhere it should not be, a phone in their hand, and no idea whose job it is. The one cause this card makes: the wrong people called first, which delays the clear while the water keeps coming (Table B emergency drainage done badly: wrong asset identification delays the responsible operator). From the trade facts ownership rows, as what usually applies and never with an Act's name: the drain serving only their home inside their boundary is usually theirs; a shared pipe, or the pipe once it is past their boundary, is usually the water company's, cleared at the company's cost; so if next door has the same problem, or the full chamber is in the road or a shared one, the water company is the first call, and if it is only their own drain, this business (Table E who to call first; the water company does not clear every private drain free). What not to do, from the rows: no chemical cleaner, no climbing into a chamber, no walking through the water with an open cut, no pumping a flooded room before the outside level has dropped. Then what to have ready for the call: which fixtures, whether the chamber is full, how long. By category: the same on every category; Sewage Disposal Service and Septic Tank Service add that a tank or a pump is private and the call is to this business. Never 'call us first' as a rule; never a time by which anyone arrives unless [CV: response_time] is set.

cards.title: The first signs
cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the trade facts signs row for this service, in their words: a sink slow to empty, a gurgle, a smell at the plughole or by the outside chamber, water standing in a gully, paving over a run that has settled, a grease layer visible, a pump alarm. The one cause this card makes: deposits narrowing the pipe over time (grease, scale, silt, solids), so each flush has less room to pass. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: specific, never alarming (the flow obstructed and waste water backing up, silt flooding the surface beside a gully, solids carried into a drainage field). cards.title: It keeps coming back
cards.brief: A drain cleared a month ago and blocked again at the same spot, a chamber that fills after every use, a tank that backs up soon after an empty, a smell that returns however often the trap is cleaned. The one cause this card makes: the blockage cleared and its cause left in place: rods that punched a hole through the obstruction and left the pipe walls coated, roots cut back that regrew into the same open joint, a trap cleaned when the fault was in the drain beyond it, a tank emptied when the field had failed (Table B done badly rows for drain unblocking, tree root removal, blocked sinks and showers and septic tank repairs). Say what the job does to get at the cause, from the trade facts stages and the pack's craft rules: the whole inside of the pipe scoured rather than a channel opened, the joint the roots came through sealed with a patch repair or a liner once the roots are out, the suspected section put under the camera so the repair is decided off what is seen. Never a dig at whoever came before. On an investigation page: the repeat is the reason for the survey, and the survey can find nothing wrong, which is a result in itself. On a schedule led page: what a visit on a regular pattern catches before it becomes a call out, with no interval unless the trade facts rows or the client values give it.
cards.mechanism: the blockage cleared and its cause left in place

cards.title: When a clear isn't the answer any more
cards.brief: The signs from the trade facts that the pipe itself has gone: the camera showing cracks or open joints, a flattened or blistered bore on a pitch fibre run, a collapsed section, a chamber wall broken, a cover that rocks, a tank cracked or discharging straight to a stream (Table B drain relining, pitch fibre drain repairs, drain excavation and replacement, manhole repairs and septic tank repairs signs rows). The one cause this card makes: a pipe that has lost its shape or its joints, which no amount of clearing puts back. Say honestly what decides between a patch, a full length liner, re rounding with a liner and a dig, from Table E: a patch treats one local fault and a liner renovates a run; a liner needs a pipe that has kept its round and can be cleaned and got into; serious deformation or collapse needs re rounding with a structural liner or replacement; re rounding on its own is not a finished repair. All of it decided off the footage, never off the symptom (Table E collapse against ordinary blockage; the pack's craft rule). On a septic page the same honesty about repairing the tank against replacing the tank or the field (Table B done badly: repairing only the tank when the field has failed). Never a lifespan or a figure the rows do not give; never 'collapsed' from a symptom; never a reline as the default.
cards.mechanism: a pipe that has lost its shape or its joints

cards.title: Water or sewage where it shouldn't be
cards.brief: Waste water pooling over a drainage field, wet or sunken ground above a run, a strip of grass greener than the rest in a dry spell, a puddle that stands by a downpipe, a gully brimming, a cellar with water in it (Table B leak detection, drain repairs, soakaways, gully cleaning, septic tank emptying and flood water pumping signs rows). The one cause this card makes: water held with no way out, or escaping where it should be held: an outlet silted up, ground that cannot take it, a joint letting it leak into the soil. Say what the job does about it from the trade facts stages for this service (the gully cleared to its outlet, the soakaway's ground tested before it is sized, the leak traced and the joint repaired, the field inspected with the tank), and what the facts say about a leak and the soil (it softens or washes away, Table E) without ever diagnosing subsidence. Not a restriction building up (card 1) and not a fault left behind (card 2): the category page owns the ground that holds the rain.

cards.title: A house with no drain to connect to
cards.brief: The customer's situation: a new build, a barn or a conversion, or a house bought off the mains with a tank nobody knows the age of; the drains have to go somewhere and there is no public sewer at the gate. What decides it: whether a sewer is within reach, because the trade facts order of choice runs public sewer first, then a suitable private one, then a treatment system, then a cesspool as the last resort (Table A septic tank and treatment plant installation: sewer availability and the discharge route assessed first; Table C with 'usually' and never the distance or the regulation's name); then the ground, the groundwater and how many people live there, which size the tank or the plant and its drainage field (Table A: flow calculated and the ground tested). What the work gives them: a system sized for the house with an outlet that is allowed, approved before it goes in and commissioned and handed over at the end (Table A stages). Leads on the Septic tank and treatment plant installation page. Never a fault invented for it; never 'your tank is illegal'; never a figure or a deadline.

cards.title: Septic tank or treatment plant
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they are choosing between a plain septic tank and a packaged treatment plant, or have been told their old tank runs straight to the stream and must change. What decides it: where the treated water can go, from the trade facts rows as what usually applies: a septic tank's outlet goes to a drainage field in ground that can take it, never to a stream; a discharge to a stream or a ditch needs a treatment plant; a tank that today discharges straight to a watercourse is connected, replaced or redirected to a drainage field, with the owner expected to plan it within a reasonable time (Table E the 2020 rule, with 'usually' and never the year, the volume or the months); and the ground test that says whether a field will work at all (Table E percolation tests: the test that suits the system). What the work gives them: the system that fits their ground and their outlet, with the approvals the rule rows ask for handled before the dig, and a pump only where gravity cannot do it (Table A materials and methods). Leads on the Septic tank and treatment plant installation page. A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. Never a product as 'the one to choose'; never a running cost or a lifespan.

cards.title: Doing it once, properly
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they have a cheaper quote, or a tank the last owner put in that has never worked right, and want to know what the difference buys. What decides it: the parts they will never see once the ground is back: the drainage field laid in tested ground at the distances the rule rows give (Table C, with 'usually' and never the figure), the outlet that matches the system, the plant sized and commissioned for the house (Table B done badly: the wrong outlet, unsuitable ground, wrong sizing or commissioning are what fail; Table A: approvals secured, ground tested, field constructed, commissioned and handed over). What the work gives them: a system that treats what the house sends it and a field that keeps taking it, with the paperwork that goes with a new system. One specific from the stages; no distance or figure the rows do not give; never a dig at another installer.
cards.mechanism: the field and the outlet they will never see once the ground is back

cards.title: What it will need from you afterwards
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want to know what they are taking on with a tank or a plant of their own. What decides it: what the system needs to keep working, from the trade facts rows: the sludge emptied before it reaches the tank's capacity, on the interval the maker's instructions give and the guidance has it (Table E septic emptying frequency, with 'usually' and never a fixed date of the business's own); the equipment kept working and repaired when it is not; the tanker firm a registered waste carrier (Table E septic sludge disposal); the system's information kept and passed on when the house is sold (Table C maintenance row). What the work gives them: an honest picture of the schedule a system runs on, and the emptying and repair pages linked where the services list has them. Never a promise about how long it lasts; never 'maintenance free'; an emptying contract only where the services list has one.

problem_card.title: Getting it in when the ground allows
problem_card.brief: The customer's situation: they want the system in before they move in, or want to know when the work can happen. What decides it: the ground and the weather, from the trade facts timing cells for this service: the work runs all year, subject to groundwater, weather and a dig that can be made safe, and the ground test is not done in a downpour, a hard frost or a drought because the result would not be true of the ground (Table A septic tank and treatment plant installation and soakaways). What the work gives them: a field tested when the test means something and a dig made when the ground will hold. No dates, nothing about spring being busy or booking ahead, no promise about the weather.

Nothing about winter being busy. No dates. This is the one place the timing is written.

cards.title: Drains laid with the street
cards.brief: A blockage that comes back on one street and never on the next, a chamber shared with the neighbours, a drain nobody has a plan of. The one cause this card makes: pipework laid when the houses went up, which the town profile dates: older streets usually drain through clay pipe laid in short lengths, often on runs shared between the houses; some post war estates used pitch fibre pipe, which the facts date by its old standards and never to an exact year; later estates are usually on plastic (the pack's section 3; Table E pitch fibre identification). Tie the era to what the work involves, never to the drains' condition: a shared run of that age is often the water company's past the boundary (the ownership rows, with 'usually'), a jointed pipe is where the camera looks first, a pitch fibre run is identified before anyone decides on a liner. Never 'the drains here are failing'; never an era as the current state (the pack's section 3 and 7). Not a fault at one point in the pipe: the category and service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: pipework laid when the houses went up

cards.title: Ground that moves the joints
cards.brief: A blockage in the same spot every winter, a dip the camera finds where nothing was dug, a joint open on a run that was sound a few years ago. The one cause this card makes: ground that shrinks and swells around the pipe, working the joints loose over the years; the town profile and a symptom say which ground (clay that shrinks in a dry summer and swells in a wet winter, made ground, a river valley). Say what it means for the work, in plain words: a jointed pipe on moving ground is the case for a camera before a reline or a dig, and a repair is decided off what the footage shows (Table E collapse against ordinary blockage). Never promise the ground will change; never a claim that the town's drains have moved. Not roots and not water the ground will not take: the other cards own those.
cards.mechanism: ground that shrinks and swells around the pipe

cards.title: Roots along the tree lined roads
cards.brief: A blockage back every few months, roots on the footage, a chamber that fills after use on a road of mature trees. The one cause this card makes: roots finding a cracked or open joint and growing into the pipe, where they hold solids and block the flow (Table B tree root removal signs and skipped rows); the town profile gives the tree lined roads and the mature gardens. Say what the work involves without claiming every drain has roots: the growth removed by cutter or jetter, after which the camera checks the opening they used and it is closed off, a local repair or a lining, since removal on its own leaves the gap for regrowth (Table A and the done badly row). Protected trees: what usually applies before a tree is touched, with 'usually' and never an order's name, only where the dossier gives the protection. Never 'drains here are full of roots' (the pack's section 3).
cards.mechanism: roots finding a cracked or open joint

cards.title: Rain the ground won't take
cards.brief: A soakaway that stops working every winter, a garden that stays waterlogged, water off a new drive running to the road or next door, a drainage field with waste water on top in a wet month. The one cause this card makes: ground or a water table that will not take the rain, which the town profile gives (a high water table, heavy clay, a flood setting, a newer estate built on soakaways, off mains villages where the research shows them). Say what it means for the work in plain words: a soakaway's ground and groundwater tested before it is sized, and not in a downpour or a frost; roof water kept out of a tank as the rule rows have it; a field on a high water table looked at with the tank. Flood history and surface water flooding only from the research; a water company named only where the research confirms it (the pack's section 3). Never a promise the ground will drain; never a claim that the town floods.

cards.brief: How much has built up, how long since the last clean, fats set hard, oil or silt taking up the room, a filter or a basket to clean (Table F grease trap: retained waste quantity, cleaning complexity; Table B: fats go solid in the pipe). There is no one legal cleaning interval: it depends on the unit and how hard it is worked (Table E), so never state one. Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: Getting to it
cards.brief: A unit behind the kitchen line or under a floor against one with a clear lid outside, how far it sits from where a tanker can park, and working round the hours the kitchen is shut (Table F grease trap: separator access; an accessible unit costs less). Say why awkward access costs more time. Hours of work only from the client values.

cards.title: Where it goes, and what the visit finds
cards.brief: What comes out is waste that has to go by the right route, and what kind of waste it is moves the price (Table F grease trap: waste classification and disposal; Table E). A registered carrier named only from the client values. A damaged part or a slow run past the unit is recorded on the visit and priced as its own job (Table A grease trap: components inspected, waste and operation recorded). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How many gullies, traps and runs are on the round
cards.brief: The number and the spread of what has to be looked after: gullies, traps, interceptors and runs, on one site or several (Table F drain maintenance contracts: how many there are and how far they spread). Accurate records and visits grouped together cost less (Table F). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: How often we come
cards.brief: How often each part of the round needs a visit, which follows how the site runs and the weather it gets, never a fixed legal interval (Table A drain maintenance contracts: visits and intervals vary, no universal standard; Table F: service frequency). A kitchen's traps against a car park's gullies. No interval stated unless [CV: price_list] or the client values give one.

cards.title: What a visit covers
cards.brief: What is on the agreed list: gully or interceptor cleaning, jetting, the camera where it is planned, the waste taken away, the defects written up (Table A drain maintenance contracts: the materials cell; Table F: waste removal, condition reporting). Traffic or access controls on a working site add to it (Table F). Say what is in and what is not.

cards.title: What the first visit finds
cards.brief: The first visit sets the baseline: what is there, whose it is and what state it is in (Table A: what is there and who answers for it mapped, its condition surveyed as a baseline). Faults from before the round started are written up and priced as their own jobs, outside the round. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us What's on the Site
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to say first: the kind of site, how many gullies, traps, interceptors and runs there are as far as anyone knows, any drainage plan or earlier reports, what keeps going wrong (repeat blockages, gullies holding water, grease or silt coming back), and who has to be told before anyone lifts a cover. No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Walk It and Price the Round
steps.brief: What gets looked at, from Table A drain maintenance contracts: what is on the site mapped and whose each part is, the state of it recorded, then what each visit covers and how often it comes set out and priced. Walking the site only from the site_visit_before_quote practice; how the price is given only from [CV: quote_method]; only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free'.

steps.title: We Visit on the Dates Agreed
steps.brief: The dates agreed in advance around how the site runs. On each visit the agreed list done, then the defects and the waste recorded and the record handed over; the round looked at again and changed if it needs to be (Table A drain maintenance contracts). A fault found is reported and priced as its own job. Never a promise that nothing will block between visits. Never mention the price.
